stated_availability: "We used the IntCal20 curve for all models (Reimer et al., 2020) using the calibration process defined in equation [3]. All data and R scripts are available on https://github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve and permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942." (p.7-8, Section 5). Also: "Appendix A. Supplementary data. Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2024.105962." (p.9). Article itself is CC BY open access; no separate licence statement found for the GitHub/Zenodo archive. [Descriptive only, per protocol §7.3 not mapped to L1-L6.]

F1.evidence: "All data and R scripts are available on https://github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve and permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942" (p.7-8) — a Zenodo DOI covers the archived compiled radiocarbon data.

F2.evidence: Zenodo deposits require structured creator/title/description metadata at minting (platform requirement); paper supplies structured article info ("Keywords: Bayesian inference, Radiocarbon dating, Diffusion of innovation, Origins of farming, Burial customs, Japan, Great Britain", p.1) alongside the archived data statement.

F3.evidence: The Zenodo DOI cited (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942) resolves to a self-referential landing page that displays its own identifier, per standard Zenodo/DataCite record structure.

F4.evidence: "...permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942" (p.7-8) — Zenodo is explicitly named, a DataCite-indexed searchable registry.

A1.evidence: Data-completeness coverage assessed as "partial" (6/11 upstream sources at Tier 0-2, 54.5%). Case study 2 burial data was "collated from different published sources and databases (Bevan et al., 2017; Bloxam, 2020; Bloxam and Parker Pearson, 2022; Healy, 2012; Mallick and Reich, 2023; Olalde et al., 2018; Wilkin, 2013; Willis et al., 2016)" (p.5), including two unpublished-access PhD theses (Bloxam 2020, UCL; Wilkin 2013, Univ. Birmingham) and a paywalled book chapter (Healy 2012, Oxbow Books) with no evidence in the paper of independent open retrievability. Per A1 cross-reference rule, coverage='partial' forces A1=0 (no ethical-restriction exception applies).

A1_1.evidence: Data archive is reached via standard open HTTPS on GitHub and Zenodo (URLs given in the availability statement, p.7-8); no proprietary client, cost, or registration is described.

A1_2.evidence: No access restriction is stated for the archived data (open CC BY article context); GitHub/Zenodo infrastructure natively supports authentication/authorisation where it would be needed, though none is invoked here.

A2.evidence: Zenodo DOI-backed records retain landing-page metadata persistently as a platform guarantee, independent of file availability; the paper names this specific permanent Zenodo record (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942, p.7-8).

I1.evidence: No statement in the paper specifies the file format of the deposited compiled radiocarbon tables (e.g., CSV vs. R-specific binary); unscoreable from the text alone.

I2.evidence: No mention of controlled vocabularies or ontologies applied to the deposited/compiled data; unscoreable.

I3.evidence: Qualified PID reference to an upstream data source used in compiling the case-study-2 dataset: "Mallick, S., Reich, D., 2023. The Allen Ancient DNA Resource (AADR): A Curated Compendium of Ancient Human Genomes. https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/FFIDCW" (references, p.10); Methods (p.5) documents provenance chains linking the compiled dataset to each named source.

R1.evidence: Plural relevant attributes documented per dataset in Methods, e.g. "We examined a total of 1479 14C dates on seed remains from Japan (n = 551, from 215 sites...) and Britain (n = 928, from 314 sites...)" with filtering thresholds and the domesticate/non-domesticate indicator-variable rule (p.5).

R1_1.evidence: No explicit data-usage licence statement found for the GitHub/Zenodo archive. The CC BY notice on p.1 ("This is an open access article under the CC BY license") and the Acknowledgements CC BY note apply to the article/Author Accepted Manuscript, not explicitly to the deposited data.

R1_2.evidence: Detailed provenance given per dataset: source citations, calibrated-probability-mass filtering thresholds ("dates with a cumulative calibrated probability mass equal to or larger than 0.5", p.5), sample-size breakdowns, and geographic/temporal exclusions (e.g. Hokkaido/Ryukyu exclusion, p.5).

R1_3.evidence: Data compiled for use with the domain-standard nimbleCarbon toolkit and calibrated with "the IntCal20 curve for all models (Reimer et al., 2020)" (p.7-8), the standard Northern Hemisphere radiocarbon calibration curve for this subfield.

F1.evidence: "All data and R scripts are available on https://github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve and permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942" (p.7-8) — the same Zenodo DOI explicitly covers the R scripts.

F2.evidence: Zenodo deposit metadata (title/creators/description, platform requirement) plus extensive in-text methodological documentation of the code: model equations [5]-[9], priors, and MCMC settings (p.5-6).

F3.evidence: Self-referential Zenodo DOI record (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942) as for data, covering the same combined data+code archive.

F4.evidence: Named on both GitHub ("https://github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve") and Zenodo ("permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942", p.7-8) — both searchable code/software registries, the latter DataCite-indexed.

A1.evidence: "All data and R scripts are available on https://github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve and permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942" (p.7-8) — an unambiguous statement that the full, self-authored codebase (hierarchical and ICAR models) is deposited; no code-specific coverage gap analogous to the data upstream-sourcing problem is evidenced (code is authored by the paper's own team, not aggregated from third parties).

A1_1.evidence: Reached via standard open HTTPS on GitHub and Zenodo; free, no proprietary client or registration described.

A1_2.evidence: No access restriction stated for the code archive; standard open-repository infrastructure natively supports authorisation where needed.

A2.evidence: Zenodo DOI-backed record persistence, as for data (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942, p.7-8).

I1.evidence: "Both the hierarchical model described in equations [5–6] and the random walk ICAR model were implemented using the NIMBLE (de Valpine et al., 2017, 2020) probabilistic programming language in R (R Core Team, 2020) and the nimbleCarbon R package (Crema, 2022b; Crema and Shoda, 2021)" (p.5-6) — R source code is inherently a formal, open, shared textual representation.

I2.evidence: No evidence of code-level controlled-vocabulary or interoperability-standard compliance beyond general use of standard R packages; unscoreable beyond what is credited under I1/R1.3.

I3.evidence: Qualified PID reference to a dependent software resource: "de Valpine, P., Adler, D., Turek, D., ... 2020. NIMBLE: MCMC, Particle Filtering, and Programmable Hierarchical Modeling. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1211190" (references, p.10), plus the IntCal20 calibration-curve citation (Reimer et al., 2020) the code depends on.

R1.evidence: Rich accompanying description of the code: model equations [5]-[9], priors ("r ~ Exponential(100)", "μ ~ Beta(2,2)", "φ ~ Gamma(5,0.1)", p.6) and full MCMC configuration ("four chains, each with 1 million iterations (half discarded as burn-in) and with thinning set to 50", p.6).

R1_1.evidence: No explicit code licence (e.g. MIT/GPL) stated anywhere in the paper text for the GitHub/Zenodo repository.

R1_2.evidence: Detailed provenance: software stack and package versions named (NIMBLE, nimbleCarbon, R), plus convergence diagnostics reported ("we evaluated the mixing of our model using the Gelman-Rubin statistic", p.6; agreement indices per Bronk Ramsey 1995).

R1_3.evidence: Uses community-recognised domain tools for Bayesian radiocarbon modelling — the nimbleCarbon package (Crema, 2022b; Crema and Shoda, 2021) built on NIMBLE, and the IntCal20 calibration curve (Reimer et al., 2020), standard practice in this subfield.
